annotation_description: MiMo Johnny already has a Living End in hand, and the mulligan choices include a second copy of Living End. Bottoming Generous Ent instead of the redundant Living End removes a valuable cycling creature (forestcycling for {1}) that both fixes mana and fills the graveyard for the Living End combo.

Playing Steam Vents as the land for turn 1 when holding Mountain and wanting to cast Preordain (U) or Mishra's Bauble (0) this turn. Steam Vents requires paying 2 life to enter untapped, and since the player likely wants to use it for blue mana to cast Preordain, they'll pay 2 life. However, the better sequencing is to play Mountain first, cast Mishra's Bauble for free (it costs 0), activate Bauble to look at opponent's top card and get a draw next upkeep, then save Steam Vents for turn 2 when they can play it untapped for Preordain. This avoids paying 2 life on turn 1 unnecessarily. Playing Mountain + Bauble turn 1, then Steam Vents (paying 2 life) + Preordain turn 2 accomplishes the same things but delays Preordain by one turn. Alternatively, if the goal is to cast Preordain turn 1 to improve card selection early, paying 2 life for Steam Vents is reasonable. But the player could also play Mountain, cast Bauble for free, and save Preordain for turn 2 with Steam Vents, potentially saving 2 life if they draw another blue source or decide to enter Steam Vents tapped on turn 2. The play is defensible but slightly suboptimal in sequencing.

Casting Mishra's Bauble before Preordain is slightly suboptimal sequencing. Preordain lets you scry 2 and draw a card, which manipulates the top of your library. If you cast Preordain first, you arrange the top of your library, and then Bauble's ability to look at the top card becomes more meaningful (or you could use Bauble on the opponent instead). By casting Bauble first and activating it, you look at a top card before you've had a chance to arrange it with Preordain's scry. However, since Bauble's draw is delayed until next upkeep, and Preordain draws immediately, the sequencing matters: casting Preordain first lets you scry 2 (putting cards on top or bottom), then you could use Bauble to look at what's now on top after the scry. That said, casting Bauble first and then Preordain also works since you can scry after looking. The key issue is that Bauble's sacrifice and look happens before Preordain's scry, so you're looking at an unmanipulated top card. This is a minor sequencing error - both plays are reasonable, but Preordain first gives slightly better information flow.

chosen_display: Mishra's Bauble — {T}, Sacrifice {this}: Look at the top card of ta... [Activate]
annotation_description: The player activated Mishra's Bauble before casting Preordain. Preordain lets you scry 2 then draw, which rearranges the top of your library. If you cast Preordain first, you can set up the top card of your library, and then use Mishra's Bauble to look at the opponent's top card (or confirm your own top card after scrying). By activating Bauble first, the information gained about the top card is wasted since Preordain's scry will rearrange those cards anyway. Additionally, Preordain could put a card on top that you want to draw next turn via Bauble's delayed draw trigger - the sequencing of Preordain first into Bauble activation would maximize information and card quality.

Playing Hedge Maze (which enters tapped) instead of Misty Rainforest on turn 1 is suboptimal. Misty Rainforest could be cracked immediately to fetch a Forest or Island (including finding a dual land like Hedge Maze itself if needed later), giving access to mana this turn. With Generous Ent in hand that has Forestcycling for {1}, having untapped mana available on turn 1 or being able to crack the fetchland at end of opponent's turn for deck thinning and shuffle effects is more flexible. Additionally, Hedge Maze's surveil 1 trigger provides marginal value, but having the fetchland in play gives more options - you can crack it later at instant speed, and on future turns you may want to play Watery Grave untapped. The sequencing of playing the tapped land first seems reasonable on the surface since you want to 'use up' the tapped-land tempo loss early, but Misty Rainforest would provide immediate mana access and better sequencing options for future turns.

Playing Monastery Swiftspear in the postcombat main phase on turn 1 means it can't attack this turn anyway, so the timing doesn't matter for combat. However, the player should have played a land (Mountain or Wooded Foothills) in addition to casting Swiftspear, since they have the land drop available and Steam Vents is already tapped. By casting Swiftspear without first playing a land, they risk forgetting the land drop. More importantly, if they play Wooded Foothills now, they can crack it on the opponent's turn to thin their deck. The sequencing of land before spell is generally correct practice, though in this specific case since Steam Vents is tapped and they're casting Swiftspear off it (it was already tapped from Preordain presumably), the land drop doesn't affect the Swiftspear cast. The real issue is that they should play a land this turn too - but looking at the choices, they can only pick one action. Actually, re-reading: the choices offered are Mountain, Wooded Foothills, or Monastery Swiftspear. They chose Swiftspear. They likely still get priority to play a land afterward. So this seems fine - casting Swiftspear with available mana and presumably playing a land next. No clear blunder here.

Playing Mountain instead of Wooded Foothills is slightly suboptimal. Wooded Foothills is better to play now because: 1) It can be cracked later to thin the deck and fix mana. 2) It puts an additional card type (land going to graveyard) toward delirium - the graveyard already has artifact (Mishra's Bauble), sorcery (Preordain), and instant (Mutagenic Growth), so sacrificing a fetchland would add 'land' as a 4th type, enabling delirium for Unholy Heat (6 damage) and Violent Urge (double strike). Playing the basic Mountain now means the fetchland played later can't enable delirium as quickly, and you lose flexibility. With Unholy Heat and Violent Urge in hand, enabling delirium should be a priority.

Casting Violent Urge post-combat on a tapped Monastery Swiftspear accomplishes almost nothing meaningful. The Swiftspear already attacked and is tapped, so first strike/double strike doesn't matter until next turn (and it's an instant, so it could be cast during next combat). The +1/+0 until end of turn is wasted since combat is over. While it does trigger prowess, there's no way to capitalize on that prowess trigger post-combat. This wastes a card that could provide significant value later - with delirium active (4+ card types in graveyard: artifact, sorcery, instant, creature from Bauble/Preordain/Mutagenic/Swiftspear), Violent Urge would grant double strike during an actual combat step, potentially dealing massive damage.

MiMo Johnny attempted to cast Generous Ent, which costs {5}{G} (6 mana), but only has 1 land on the battlefield (Hedge Maze, which is tapped). There is no way to pay for this spell. Additionally, even if they could cast spells, they should be playing a land first (Misty Rainforest or Watery Grave) before casting any spells to maximize available mana. The game engine appears to have let this through somehow, but choosing an uncastable 6-mana creature when you have 1 land is nonsensical. They should have played a land (Misty Rainforest or Watery Grave) to develop their mana base toward eventually casting their spells.

MiMo Johnny skipped their land drop on turn 2 with three lands in hand (Misty Rainforest, Watery Grave, Breeding Pool). This is a Living End cascade deck that needs to reach 3 mana to cast Shardless Agent (1GU) on turn 3 to cascade into Living End. With only one land (Hedge Maze) on the battlefield, skipping this land drop means they can't cast Shardless Agent on turn 3, delaying their key combo by at least a turn. Against an aggressive Monastery Swiftspear deck that's already dealt significant damage, every turn matters.

Played Watery Grave (U/B) when Breeding Pool (G/U) would have been better. The B mana from Watery Grave isn't needed now (Living End will be cascaded into, not hardcast), while Breeding Pool directly provides both colors for the key turn 3 Shardless Agent ({1}{G}{U}). Playing Watery Grave wastes the B mana color and reserves less flexible lands for later.

Playing Breeding Pool instead of Overgrown Tomb means MiMo Johnny only has one black source (Watery Grave), making it impossible to cast Overlord of the Balemurk ({3}{B}{B}) on turn 5 without drawing another black source. Both lands equally enable Formidable Speaker this turn.

Playing Formidable Speaker puts a creature on the battlefield that would be sacrificed when Living End resolves, working against the deck's primary game plan. Additionally, Overlord of the Balemurk cast for its impending cost ({1}{B}) would mill 4 cards into the graveyard (fueling Living End) and return a creature like Shardless Agent from the graveyard to hand, while staying as a non-creature enchantment that survives Living End.

message: Discard a card and search your library for a creature card, reveal it, put it into your hand, then shuffle?
annotation_description: Discarding Living End instead of Overlord of the Balemurk to Formidable Speaker's tutor ability. Overlord in the graveyard would make Living End significantly more powerful when cascaded into, bringing back a 5/5 creature. Living End can't be hardcast and having two copies in hand is redundant.

Opponent has zero creatures on the battlefield to block. Attacking with only Generous Ent deals 5 damage instead of 7. The extra 2 damage from Formidable Speaker is free since there are no blockers, and Formidable Speaker's tap ability can't be activated anyway (no untapped mana available). Against a burn-heavy opponent at 13 life while at 8 life yourself, every point of pressure matters.

Attacked with only the Monk Token (2/2 with trample) into Formidable Speaker (2/4), which can block and kill it while taking no trample damage. Meanwhile, Slickshot Show-Off has flying and would deal 1 guaranteed unblockable damage to the opponent at 5 life. The Monk Token is likely to die for nothing if blocked.

At 5 life facing 3 damage from two attackers (Monk Token 2/2 and Slickshot Show-Off 1/2), MiMo Johnny did not block with available creatures (Formidable Speaker 2/4 and potentially Endurance 3/4). Taking unnecessary damage at such a low life total against a burn deck is dangerous.
